stories.headline: WTI TOPS $104, STOCKS FALL FOR A FOURTH STRAIGHT SESSION
stories.body: WTI crude settled up 8.06% to roughly $104 a barrel and Brent pushed above $107, both the highest closes since spring, as an escalating Middle East war raised fears of disrupted supply. The S&P 500 fell 0.58% to 7,591.70 and the Nasdaq-100 dropped 1.08% to 29,104, marking a fourth consecutive down day for the major averages.
stories.explain: Oil is a direct input cost across the economy — transportation, plastics, agriculture, shipping — so a move above $100 raises headline and core inflation expectations right as the Fed weighs its next move. Higher expected inflation pushes up the term premium investors demand on long-dated Treasuries, which raises the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings and compresses equity valuations even before a single company's profit outlook changes. That's the direct mechanical link between a war half a world away and a red day on the S&P.

stories.headline: HOT PPI SENDS 10-YEAR YIELD TO 4.94%, PUSHES FED HIKE ODDS TO 73%
stories.body: August producer prices rose 0.4% month-over-month as expected, but the year-over-year rate jumped to 5.4% from 4.8% in July — hotter than forecast. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped 11 basis points to 4.94%, its highest level since October 2023, and CME FedWatch now prices a 73% probability of a quarter-point hike at next week's FOMC meeting, with Friday's CPI report (consensus +0.4% MoM, +3.4% YoY) seen as the deciding factor.
stories.explain: PPI measures price changes at the wholesale level before they reach consumers, so an accelerating year-over-year print signals cost pressure is still building in the pipeline rather than fading — the opposite of what the Fed wants to see this late in a cycle. Fed-hike odds are priced directly off the fed funds futures curve, and a hawkish repricing there (a hike where a hold was expected weeks ago) forces a rapid revaluation of rate-sensitive assets, hitting long-duration growth stocks hardest. The Fed's dilemma is that a supply shock (oil) is doing the inflationary work that would normally require excess demand, and rate hikes are a blunt tool against a supply problem.

stories.headline: GOLD SINKS 2% AS SURGING YIELDS AND A STRONGER DOLLAR OVERPOWER SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND
stories.body: Gold fell 2.06% to roughly $4,360 an ounce even as war fears intensified, as the DXY dollar index rose 0.36% to 99.09 and the 10-year yield's jump to 4.94% raised the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset.
stories.explain: Gold typically benefits from geopolitical fear, but it also competes directly with Treasuries for safe-haven capital — and Treasuries now yield nearly 5% with no storage cost. When real and nominal yields spike alongside a stronger dollar, that combination usually overwhelms any war-driven safe-haven bid, because gold pays no coupon and a stronger dollar makes it more expensive for foreign buyers. Today's move shows the rates channel currently dominating the geopolitical-fear channel in gold's price action.

stories.headline: ORACLE JUMPS 6% AFTER-HOURS ON EARNINGS BEAT
stories.body: Oracle reported fiscal Q1 adjusted EPS of $1.92 and revenue of $19.35 billion, both ahead of Street estimates, sending shares up roughly 6% in extended trading even as the broader market closed lower for a fourth straight session.
stories.explain: Oracle's cloud infrastructure backlog is watched as a bellwether for AI-driven capital spending, so a beat here reassures investors that hyperscaler demand — a key pillar of the broader 'AI trade' — remains intact even as macro headwinds like oil and yields weigh on the index-level tape. The after-hours pop illustrates how a strong idiosyncratic result can decouple from a market selloff driven by top-down macro forces rather than company fundamentals.

stories.headline: FOURTH STRAIGHT LOSING SESSION AS OIL, RATES AND INFLATION FEARS COMPOUND
stories.body: Thursday marked a fourth consecutive down day for the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq as investors absorbed the combination of $100-plus oil, a 10-year yield near a three-year high, and a hotter-than-expected wholesale inflation print — all landing one day before Friday's CPI report and roughly a week before the Fed's next rate decision.
stories.explain: When several negative catalysts compound in the same week — a supply shock, a hawkish repricing of Fed odds, and rising discount rates — index-level losses tend to understate how much of the move is concentrated in the most rate-sensitive, highest-multiple names. That's why watching sector dispersion beneath the headline index number, not just the S&P's daily percentage change, tends to say more about which risk is actually driving the tape.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S FORWARD BABACAR SANE GRANTED ELIGIBILITY VIA COURT ORDER
stories.body: A judge issued a temporary restraining order clearing St. John's forward Babacar Sane to play this season, the latest example of players using antitrust and due-process challenges to fight NCAA eligibility rulings as the 2026-27 season approaches its November tip-off.

stories.headline: NBA RELEASES FULL 2026 PRESEASON SLATE AS OFFSEASON MOVES CONTINUE
stories.body: The league's preseason schedule tips off October 3 with Heat-Raptors in Quebec City and wraps October 16 with a Nuggets-Lakers matchup on ESPN. Houston's Fred VanVleet opted into his $25 million player option, while the offseason's two biggest storylines — LeBron James joining Philadelphia and Giannis Antetokounmpo teaming with Miami — continue to reshape title odds ahead of training camp.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS SURVIVE WITHOUT DARNOLD, TOP PATRIOTS 13-10 IN SUPER BOWL REMATCH
stories.body: Backup Drew Lock led Seattle to a 13-10 win over New England in the NFL's Wednesday-night kickoff game after starter Sam Darnold exited with a hip injury. The defending Super Bowl champions open 2026 at 1-0, though Darnold could miss multiple weeks.

stories.headline: NO. 7 MIAMI HOSTS FAMU IN WEEK 2 HOME OPENER AT HARD ROCK STADIUM
stories.body: Miami, ranked No. 7 in the AP poll, plays its first home game of the season Thursday night against Florida A&M as Week 2 gets underway. Elsewhere, Rutgers turns to first-time starter AJ Surace at quarterback for Friday's trip to Boston College.

deepDive.title: Why a War-Driven Oil Spike Is the Fed's Hardest Inflation Problem
content: Today's selloff wasn't primarily an earnings story — it was a supply story. WTI settled up 8.06% near $104 a barrel after Middle East hostilities threatened tanker traffic and export infrastructure, and that single move did more damage to sentiment than any single company's guidance. It landed one day before Friday's CPI print and about a week before the Fed's next meeting, where the market now prices a 73% chance of a hike rather than a hold — a scenario that looked remote just weeks ago. Understanding why an oil shock moves a central bank matters more right now than tracking the shock itself.

The mechanism runs through the CPI basket and the term premium. Energy carries a direct weight in headline CPI, and a sustained move above $100 WTI typically shows up in gasoline and utility prices within four to eight weeks, plus a slower indirect drag through transportation and input costs across nearly every other good. Today's producer price data already shows that pass-through beginning: the year-over-year PPI rate jumped to 5.4% from 4.8% in July. When traders expect that pipeline pressure to reach consumers, they demand more compensation for holding longer-dated bonds, pushing the 10-year yield to 4.94% — its highest since October 2023 — independent of anything the Fed has actually done yet.

What's easy to miss is that supply-shock inflation and demand-shock inflation are economically different problems, even though they show up as the same CPI number. During the 1973 and 1979 oil embargoes, the Fed initially tried to treat the price jump as a one-time level shift rather than a lasting inflation problem — in both cases, that judgment proved wrong once elevated prices started shifting the public's inflation expectations. Once expectations de-anchor, a central bank loses the option to 'look through' the shock, because the cost of doing nothing becomes a wage-price spiral rather than a temporary price bump. Rate hikes don't fix a broken oil supply chain; they work by crushing demand hard enough elsewhere in the economy to offset it.

That's the lens for the next week. Friday's CPI print will show how much of this oil move has already passed through, but the number that matters more is what happens to inflation expectations, not the headline print itself. If expectations stay anchored, the Fed still has room to treat oil as a transitory shock even with wholesale prices running hot. If they don't, a hike becomes very hard to avoid — and today's move in gold, which fell 2% even as war fears intensified, suggests the market is already leaning toward the second outcome: yields and the dollar rising faster than fear can push safe-haven demand higher.
